newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW - Helix feels the heat.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Helix feels the heat.

text.p: Helix Resources Ltd managing director Rob Mosig, who holds prime ground in Australia's latest gold hot spot - the remote and barren Gawler Craton in north-west South Australia - is between a rock and a hard place.

All eyes will be on Helix later this month when it releases its latest quarterly exploration report and Mosig feels the market is looking for multi-million ounce deposits in ground which remains barely tested or properly understood.

"We are not even into six months of age for the project and you cannot (in that time period) get the type of results that the market is waiting for in general terms from a region such as this," Mosig told Reuters in an interview.
Helix shares surged last year from 45 cents to A$4.99 in just four months on top of promising results at its Tunkillia prospect in the searing desert of north-west South Australia.
But the stock was savaged on disappointment with interim results released in February and has steadily slid back since, closing on Wednesday at A$1.78.
The latest result saw average grades of about 0.7 grams per tonne of gold, against the earlier grades of about 2.0 g/t.
One analyst, who did not want to be named, said the market was clearly looking for substantial results from Helix in the next quarterly report, due out around April 28.

"You are looking for broad intercepts of moderate grades at least, and that I think would give the market a little bit more confidence to build on ... but clearly in this environment, in this market, people are a little bit wary," he said.
Mosig admits to coming under some heavy pressure in recent weeks, with investors angry about the weaker results and share price fall and with analysts polarised on Helix's value.
"Analysts are nuts and bolts sort of people, they like to crunch numbers and it is impossible with the data that Helix has at the moment to crunch sensible numbers," he said.
He said Helix's price, like gold exploration stocks worldwide, had been further undermined by controversy swirling around Canada's Bre-X Minerals Ltd.
Bre-X said last month that it was possible the amount of gold in the Busang gold deposit in Indonesia - rated the greatest find this century - had been overrated.

Mosig said Helix was boosting exploration work at the Lake Everard tenement to A$1 million a month and currently had two reverse circulation rigs, one diamond drill and one rotary air blast drill working around the major gold target of Area 223.

"Overall we are relatively pleased with everything, nothwithstanding the Busang disaster and the sharemarket response in Australia, notwithstanding analysts' reports (devaluing Helix's price)," he said.
Helix, he said, still believed Tunkillia had the potential to show a world class deposit, a multi-million ounce resource.
But he is seeking to dampen expectations of immediate major success, given the deep sandy cover and lack of outcrop of the Gawler Craton, seen by many as Australia's last gold frontier.

"We are working with nothing other than the third dimension, drill holes, there is no information from surface that we can use. It requires time, it requires money and it requires good technical expertise to do that," he said.
With Helix's quarterly report to produce progress on around April 28, Mosig said the market should be judging the company's exploration programme and continuity of mineralisation.

"We have a zone that goes eight kilometres in the western part of the Tunkillia anomaly and within that we (believe) there will be repeats to the area 223 mineralisation ... and confident there will be further deposits as we address the rest of the 25 square kilometres of the anomaly," he said.
Helix received a voted of confidence in February when Acacia Resources Ltd bought a 17.4 percent stake for A$38 million or A$4.45 a share.
Acacia's share price has fallen sharply since then to close at A$1.82 on Wednesday, down from a year high of A$2.45.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
